sections.p16.s0: The layers under Python. Items 0 to 4 cover C and the machine: write, compile and run a small C program for each, on Linux or WSL. Items 5 to 9 cover how CPython runs your code: test each idea in the REPL. Spend about 60 per cent of the phase here.
sections.p16.s1: Five hands-on exercises that apply the Learn section. Do them in order, since items 1 and 2 use the same hot function. Record every prediction and measurement in one notes file so you can compare them later.

p16.s0.0.how: Work through CS50 week 1 or the first chapters of Beej's Guide to C, typing and compiling each example. Then open a short CPython file such as Objects/boolobject.c and annotate every declaration, type, loop and function call.
p16.s0.0.done: You can read a 100-line C function and describe what it does, including its types, control flow and return values.

p16.s0.1.how: Write C programs that swap two ints through pointers, walk an array with pointer arithmetic, and print element addresses with %p. Compile with gcc -Wall -g -fsanitize=address, add an out-of-bounds write, and read the sanitiser report.
p16.s0.1.done: You can explain why a[i] is *(a + i) and predict the address step between elements of an int and a double array.

p16.s0.2.how: Write a function that returns a pointer to a local array and observe the bug, then fix it with malloc and free. Add a leak and a double free on purpose, and run each version under Valgrind or AddressSanitizer.
p16.s0.2.done: You can say which values live on the stack and which on the heap in a given function, and your fixed program runs clean under Valgrind.

p16.s0.3.how: On Linux or WSL, run strace -f python3 -c "open('x.txt', 'w').write('hi')" and find the openat, write and close calls. Run it again with strace -c for a summary, then repeat using os.open and os.write.
p16.s0.3.done: You can name the system calls behind a Python file write and explain what the kernel does that user code cannot.

p16.s0.4.how: Compile a two-file C program in stages: gcc -E, gcc -S, gcc -c, then link. Inspect the object files with nm and objdump -d, remove one function definition, and read the undefined-reference error from the linker.

where.name: GCC: Options controlling the kind of output

p16.s0.4.done: You can explain preprocessing, compiling, assembling and linking, and fix an undefined-reference error without searching.

p16.s0.5.how: Run dis.dis on five of your own functions: a loop, a list comprehension, a closure, a try/except and an f-string. Look up each unfamiliar opcode in the dis documentation and note what it does to the value stack.

where.name: Python: dis, disassembler for Python bytecode

p16.s0.5.done: You can read a short disassembly aloud and explain what LOAD_FAST, BINARY_OP and CALL do to the stack.

p16.s0.6.how: Read the PyObject and PyVarObject sections of the C API object structures page, then Include/object.h in the CPython source. In the REPL, compare sys.getsizeof for an int, an empty list, a list of ten items and a class instance, and explain each size.

where.name: Python C API: Common object structures

p16.s0.6.done: You can name the two header fields of every PyObject in the default build (reference count and type pointer) and how type(x) is found.

p16.s0.7.how: Watch sys.getrefcount change as you bind and delete names for a list. Then build a two-object cycle, delete the names, and use a weakref.finalize callback to show it is freed only by gc.collect(). Read the gc docs for your exact 3.14 point release.
p16.s0.7.done: You can explain why reference counting alone cannot free a cycle and how the generations decide what the collector scans.

p16.s0.8.how: Read NumPy's 'What is NumPy?' page and the first section of Extending Python with C. Time a Python loop that sums a million floats against built-in sum on a list and np.sum on an array, and account for the gap.

where.name: Python: Extending Python with C or C++

p16.s0.8.done: Using your timings, you can explain the gap in terms of boxed objects, per-element interpreter dispatch and contiguous memory.

p16.s0.9.how: Read the free-threading HOWTO and PEP 779. Install the free-threaded 3.14 build (python3.14t), check sys._is_gil_enabled(), and run a CPU-bound function on 1 and 4 threads on both builds. Record wall time for each.

where.name: Python: Python support for free threading

p16.s0.9.done: You can state your measured thread speed-up and single-thread slowdown, and why an extension not marked safe re-enables the GIL.

p16.s1.0.how: Write three functions, for example a nested loop, a with block and a generator. Write down the opcodes you expect for each, then run dis.dis and mark every difference with its reason.

where.name: Python: dis, disassembler for Python bytecode

p16.s1.0.done: At least one prediction matches the real opcode sequence in full, and every miss has a written reason.

p16.s1.1.how: Profile one of your projects with cProfile and pick a hot, numeric, pure-Python function. Rewrite it as a Cython module with typed variables, or as a C extension using PyArg_ParseTuple, build it, and keep the Python version beside it.

where.name: Python: Extending Python with C or C++

p16.s1.1.done: The compiled module imports, and a test shows it returns identical results to the Python version on the same inputs.

p16.s1.2.how: Benchmark both versions with pyperf, or timeit with several repeats, on the same inputs at three or more sizes including a tiny one. Report the median and spread, and note the machine, Python version and build flags.
p16.s1.2.done: A table shows median and spread per input size, and you can say where call overhead cancels the speed-up.

p16.s1.3.how: Create a list and print sys.getrefcount after binding it to a second name, storing it in a dict, appending it to another list, and deleting each of those references in turn. Write your predicted count before each line runs.
p16.s1.3.done: Your predicted change matches every step, and you can explain the extra reference held by the getrefcount argument.

p16.s1.4.how: Build parent-child trees where each child holds a strong reference to its parent. With gc.disable(), create and drop many trees while taking tracemalloc snapshots. Confirm the cycle with gc.get_referrers, then store the parent as a weakref.ref.
p16.s1.4.done: Before the fix memory grows with each batch; after it, tracemalloc shows memory flat across 100,000 trees with the collector disabled.
